title: R' Beroka Chozaah
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: Model-assisted translation, editorially reviewed; publication authorized by Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: Taanit 22a relates that Eliyahu was frequently with him. Once he was standing in the market of Bei Lafat and asked Eliyahu whether there was anyone in the market destined for the world to come. He said to him, “No.” Meanwhile he saw a man wearing black shoes — he said to him, “This one is destined for the world to come.” He ran after him — and asked him to tell him what his deeds were. Meanwhile two brothers came; Eliyahu said to him, “These too are destined for the world to come.”

Hyman reports that Seder HaDorot cites from Yuchasin “R' Beroka said: Rav” and writes “I have not found it.” Hyman says, with respect, that an error issued from the ruler, for Yuchasin cites the wording “R' Beroka said: Rav Beroka Chozaah,” and Seder HaDorot thought they were two matters: “R' Beroka said: Rav,” and afterward “Beroka Chazua.” Hyman insists: But the truth is that Yuchasin means as follows: R' Beroka: (said) Rav Beroka Chozaah; and so it is cited in Yuchasin HaShalem, except that there the reading is that he was standing in the market designated ר׳ אלישפט.

notes.text: Hyman argues that the quoted Yuchasin heading was misread as a Rav transmission. His reported market designation ר׳ אלישפט is retained literally rather than establishing a person Rabbi Elishafat; that unresolved name/locator question stays held in p002.

Taanit 22a gives the market as Bei Lafat and continues from the man in black shoes to his work and the two brothers. The translation follows Hyman’s abridged account.

The earlier notes record the limits of the evidence then available. The London 1857 Yuchasin HaShalem (p. 121) prints the heading R’ Beroka, a colon, and “said Rav Beroka Chozaah,” with “said” abbreviated. It gives the market wording ר׳ אלישפט, which is retained literally. Seder HaDorot reads “Rav Beroka said Rav,” followed by the abbreviation for “I have not found it.” Hyman’s page prints the parenthesized “said” in his explanation. The supplied short form Chazua is retained, although the printed Hyman (vol. I, p. 294) has Chozaah there.
